articles.title: High-achieving working mothers face harsher moral judgments for parenting mistakes
articles.summary: Working mothers who pursue career success are harshly judged for their parenting mistakes, while high-achieving fathers face no such scrutiny. A new study reveals how workplace ambition triggers moral condemnation that forces women to self-regulate.

articles.title: Learning a new skill triggers both temporary cell swelling and lasting structural growth in the human brain
articles.summary: When you learn a new skill, your brain undergoes physical changes. A new study using advanced MRI technology reveals that mastering a task triggers two distinct, unexpected cellular reactions that reshape our understanding of human neuroplasticity.

articles.title: APOE2 may protect the brain from Alzheimer’s and aging
articles.summary: The longevity-linked APOE2 gene appears to protect brain cells by reducing DNA damage and helping neurons recover from stress. The finding could open a new path toward treatments that mimic APOE2’s defenses in people at higher genetic risk for Alzheimer’s.

articles.title: New study links digital “brain rot” to a cascading sequence of psychological burdens
articles.summary: The passive consumption of endless short-form videos creates cognitive fatigue popularly known as brain rot. A new study reveals how this digital exhaustion initiates a psychological cascade of burnout, stress, and anxiety that ultimately precipitates depression.

articles.title: The psychological power of naming legislation after victims
articles.summary: Lawmakers frequently name bills after victims of tragic events to rally public support. A new psychology study reveals that attaching a personal narrative to proposed legislation reliably boosts voter approval, driven largely by feelings of sympathy.

articles.title: Watching too much TV in midlife may shrink the brain
articles.summary: Watching television very often in midlife may be linked to troubling brain changes decades later. In a study of about 1,700 adults, frequent TV viewers later showed smaller brain regions involved in memory, decision-making, and visual processing, along with more signs of damage in the brain’s white matter. Surprisingly, sitting itself did not appear to be the main issue, since people who spent long hours seated at mentally engaging jobs often showed healthier brain patterns.

articles.title: Magic mushrooms may reshape the brain long after the trip ends
articles.summary: A single dose of psilocybin produced measurable changes in brain activity and possible changes in brain structure that lasted for up to a month. Participants who experienced the greatest increase in flexible, varied brain activity also reported more personal insight and later improvements in well-being. The findings suggest that the psychedelic experience itself may help people break free from entrenched patterns of thinking.

articles.title: Extreme heat takes a severe toll on mental health
articles.summary: As global temperatures climb, extreme heat is doing more than harming physical health. A new review suggests that rising temperatures degrade mood, increase aggression, and worsen preexisting psychiatric conditions, representing a growing crisis for human mental well-being.

articles.title: Thinking a date likes you makes you like them more—but it won’t win them over
articles.summary: In the fast-paced world of speed-dating, believing your date likes you makes you more likely to pursue them. However, a new study reveals that to actually win their affection, accurately guessing how they perceive you matters much more.
